title: Burrata con pesche
subtitle: Burrata with ripe peaches, prosciutto, and basil
excerpt: A whole burrata broken open at the table and served with ripe white or yellow peaches, thin slices of prosciutto crudo, fresh basil, and a drizzle of good extra-virgin olive oil. A peak-summer Italian antipasto that requires nothing more than good ingredients.
sourceNotes: Burrata con pesche is a contemporary Italian antipasto preparation built on the traditional pairing of fresh cheese with seasonal fruit that runs through Italian regional cooking from north to south. Burrata itself originates from Puglia (documented from the early twentieth century in Andria) and the pairing of its creamy interior with seasonal summer fruit is a natural extension of Italian antipasto traditions. The combination appears in Pugliese and Campanian restaurants from the 1990s onwards.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: This dish cannot be made ahead: burrata must be served immediately once cut, as it collapses. Slice the peaches and arrange everything just before sitting down.

glossaryTerms.definition: A fresh Italian cheese made from mozzarella and cream. The outside is a shell of fresh mozzarella; the inside is soft, creamy stracciatella and cream. When cut, the cream flows out. Burrata is eaten the day it is made or within 24 hours.

content.text: This dish only works when every ingredient is at its absolute best. The

must be very fresh, ideally from that day. The peaches must be ripe enough that their juice runs when sliced. The prosciutto should be cut thin at a deli rather than bought pre-packed. The olive oil must be one you would eat on bread. If any of these four things is not right, the dish will be mediocre. When they are all right, it is one of the best things you can put on a table.

items.prepNote: ripe, white or yellow, halved and stoned, each half cut into 4 wedges

content.text: Arrange the peach wedges on a large platter or divide between four plates. Lay the prosciutto in loose, informal folds between the peach pieces.

Pat the burrata dry with kitchen paper and place one per two people at the centre of the plate or platter. Score the top of each burrata with a small cross; the cream will begin to flow out at the table.
Scatter the basil leaves over everything. Drizzle generously with the olive oil. Season with sea salt flakes and a little black pepper. Serve immediately with good bread.

items.cause: Not fresh enough; bought too many days in advance
items.fix: Burrata should be eaten within 24 hours of being made. Buy it the morning you intend to serve it. If not available fresh, use very fresh buffalo mozzarella instead.

items.cause: Not ripe, or refrigerated and not brought back to room temperature
items.fix: Never refrigerate peaches intended for eating raw. Buy them a day or two before and let them ripen at room temperature on the counter.

content.text: Burrata originates in Puglia, specifically from the area around Andria. The combination of burrata with prosciutto and summer fruit is a refinement of the classic caprese concept. It appears at outdoor summer suppers from the Adriatic to the Tyrrhenian coast. In London, Sydney, and New York restaurants, burrata with seasonal accompaniments has become the defining Italian restaurant starter of the past twenty years. At home it is not really a recipe so much as an assembly. Its quality depends entirely on the quality of its three or four components.
